senses.gloss:
Loka denotes ‘world’ in the Rigveda^1 and later.^2 Mention
is often made of the three worlds,^3 and ayaṃ lokaḥ, ‘this
world,’^4 is constantly opposed to asau lokaḥ,^5 ‘yonder world’
-i.e., ‘heaven.’ Loka itself sometimes means ‘heaven,’^6
while in other passages several different sorts of world are
mentioned.^7
1) Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary,
s.v. 2, quotes no example of this mean-
ing for the Rigveda, where he sees the
word used only in the sense of ‘place,’
‘room,’ ‘free or open space.’ But Rv.
x. 14, 9, is a fairly certain example of
the wider sense.
2) Av. viii. 9, 1. 15; iv. 38, 5; xi. 5, 7;
8, 10, etc.; in ix. 5, 14, the worlds of
heaven (divya) and of earth (pārthiva)
are distinguished; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā,
xxxii. 11 et seq., etc.
3) Av. x. 6, 31; xii. 3, 20; Aitareya
Brāhmaṇa, i. 5, 8; Satapatha Brāh-
maṇa, xiii. 1, 7, 3, etc.
4) Av. v. 30, 17; viii. 8, 8; xii. 5, 38;
xix. 54, 5; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 46,
etc.
5) Av. xii. 5, 38. 57; Taittirīya Saṃ-
hitā, i. 5, 9, 4; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,
v. 28, 2; viii. 2, 3, etc.
6) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 1, 7;
x. 5, 4, 16; xi. 2, 7, 19; and so probably
Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 13, 12.
7) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxvi. 4; Kauṣī
taki Brāhmaṇa, xx. 1; Bṛhadāraṇyaka
Upaniṣad, iii. 6, 1; iv. 3, 36 et seq.;
vi. 1, 18, etc.
